newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to close loopholes in immigration law.
newsitem.headline: France to close loopholes in immigration law.

text.p: France is to review controversial immigration laws to resolve legal headaches which embarrassed the government during recent protests by African immigrants, a leading newspaper said on Tuesday.

The daily Le Monde said Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre would soon propose a new bill plugging loopholes in tough 1993 immigration laws which deprived some immigrants of residence rights without allowing authorities to expel them.
No official comment was immediately available on the report.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe said last week he would propose bills to modify the legislation on immigration and crack down on sweatshops employing clandestine immigrants.
Under pressure from the far-right, the centre-right government has vowed a crackdown on clandestine immigration.
Le Monde said the bill would make it easier to expel illegal immigrants while closing legal loopholes in favour of immigrants.
The legal headaches were highlighted in a protest by some 300 Africans who occupied a Paris church for two months this summer, claiming the 1993 laws had plunged them into illegality.
The government granted residence permits to many of them on humanitarian grounds, but many others are still waging court battles to avoid expulsion.
Le Monde said the new bill would give residence rights to illegal immigrants whose children were born in France.

Under current laws, such immigrants face a Catch 22 situation -- they may be thrown out of the country while their children may not. Lawyers have successfully fought expulsion by arguing it would violate a European convention guaranteeing the right to family life.

Under the new bill, spouses of French citizens, foreigners making a living in France for the past 15 years without residence permits, and foreigners who would face serious danger if deported home would also get residence permits.

On the other hand, the bill would make it easier for authorities to carry out expulsions by doubling to 48 hours the period for which a foreigner may be held before a judge rules on the legality of his detention.
It would also let authorities hold any suspected illegal immigrant until an appeal has been heard against a judge's decision to release him. In any case, detention would not exceed 10 days.
